The FOMC’s intermeeting 50 bp cut to a 1.00–1.25% target range, paired with lowering IOER to 1.10% and continuing T-bill purchases and repo operations to keep reserves ample, aligns with New Keynesian guidance to act preemptively when downside risks rise and inflation is muted. Clarida, Galí, and Gertler (1999) show that rules-based, forward-looking easing (Taylor-rule-consistent) helps stabilize output and inflation when shocks hit demand, while Goodfriend (2002) emphasizes that interest-on-reserves frameworks and active Desk operations efficiently anchor short rates and support policy transmission. The liquidity backstops echo Bagehot’s lender-of-last-resort principles and mitigate money market pressures, consistent with evidence that easing supports financial conditions and real activity (Romer and Romer; Christiano, Eichenbaum, and Evans). Although COVID-19 represented a mixed demand- and supply-side shock via supply-chain disruptions, the Committee’s “act as appropriate” stance and continued asset purchases/operations also work through expectations (Cochrane and Piazzesi; forward guidance literature), partially offsetting the drag. Overall tone: risk-aware but decisively accommodative, with supportive implications for the outlook despite clear near-term headwinds.
